content: Citronella oil is an essential oil derived from the leaves and stems of various species of the Cymbopogon plant. It is widely utilized as a source of perfumery chemicals, including citronellal, citronellol, and geraniol, which are extensively employed in the production of soaps, perfumes, cosmetics, and flavoring agents globally. Additionally, citronella oil is a well-known plant-based insect repellent and has been registered for this purpose in the United States since 1948. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) classifies citronella oil as a biopesticide with a non-toxic mechanism of action. Scientific studies have also demonstrated that citronella oil possesses potent antifungal properties and can be effective in calming barking dogs. Citronella oil is commercially categorized into two chemotypes: 1. Ceylon Type: This type is derived from Cymbopogon nardus Rendle and contains the following chemical composition: Geraniol: 18-20% Limonene: 9-11% Methyl isoeugenol: 7-11% Citronellol: 6-8% Citronellal: 5-15% 2. Java Type: This type is obtained from Cymbopogon winterianus Jowitt and has the following chemical composition: Citronellal: 32-45% Geraniol: 11-13% Geranyl acetate: 3-8% Limonene: 1-4% The Java type is considered superior for the production of perfumery derivatives due to its higher concentrations of geraniol and citronellal. The name Cymbopogon winterianus was given to this variety in honor of Mr. Winter, a prominent oil distiller in Ceylon who first cultivated and distilled the Maha Pangeri variety of citronella in the region. Both the Ceylon and Java types are believed to have originated from Mana Grass in Ceylon. According to Finnemore (1962), Mana Grass exists in two wild forms: Cymbopogon nardus var. linnae (typicus) and C. nardus var. confertiflorus. However, neither of these wild forms is significantly used for oil distillation. It is important to note that citronella oil derived from Cymbopogon species should not be confused with other lemon-scented oils, such as those from Corymbia citriodora or Pelargonium citrosum. Globally, the annual production of citronella oil is approximately 7,000 tonnes. The primary producers include Taiwan, Guatemala, Honduras, Indonesia, Brazil, China, Sri Lanka, India, Argentina, Ecuador, Madagascar, Mexico, and the West Indies. Citronella oil is particularly popular as a natural insect repellent. Its efficacy in repelling mosquitoes, including Aedes aegypti, has been scientifically validated. However, most citronella-based repellents applied to the skin require reapplication every 30 to 60 minutes to maintain their effectiveness. While citronella oil is generally considered safe, it may cause skin irritation or dermatitis in some individuals. It is not recommended for use on the skin of young children under the age of three. According to the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), citronella oil exhibits minimal or no toxicity when used as a topical insect repellent, with no significant adverse effects reported over a 60-year period. When used as directed, citronella oil is not expected to pose health risks to humans, including children and other sensitive populations. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) classifies citronella oil as Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS). In Canada, regulatory concerns regarding citronella oil as an insect repellent are primarily due to gaps in toxicological data rather than documented incidents. In Europe, Ceylon-type citronella oil is categorized as a Class 3 substance due to safety concerns related to its methyl eugenol content.
